newsitem.title: GERMANY: New models boost BMW's 9-month sales 8.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: New models boost BMW's 9-month sales 8.5 pct.

text.p: New models hitting the market this year boosted Bayerische Motoren-Werke (BMW) sales 8.5 percent during the first nine months of 1996, setting the stage for a satisfactory year, the carmaker said Monday.
BMW said strong demand for its new Z3 roadster sports car and the 5-Series sedan, along with brisk demand for several Rover Group Plc models, underpinned the sales growth.
"Business developments at BMW seem set to continue on their satisfactory course for the rest of 1996," the company said in a statement.
BMW said group sales climbed to 863,037 units from 795,522, lifting revenue 10.6 percent to 37.5 billion marks ($24.8 billion).

BMW cars posted a strong 8.4 percent sales increase to 486,130 units. The company said demand for the Z3 has been so strong that it has stopped producing 3-series cars at its plant in Spartanburg S.C., devoting all that factory's production to the Z3.

The 5-series model, the mid-sized car in BMW's fleet, chalked up a 47.9 percent increase to 138,948 -- an achievement made possible only by BMW's ability to reach maximum production capacity for the strong-selling car in a record amount of time.

Sales of the BMW's top-of-the-line 7-series and its entry-level 3-series both declined. The 7-series was hit by a change on taxes on company cars in Germany, while the 3-series, a top seller for years, has neared the end of its production cycle. 3-series sales fell 1.9 percent to 308,849 units.
BMW's British unit, Rover Group, reported that deliveries climbed 8.6 percent to 376,907, with Land Rover deliveries climbing 13 percent.
Demand for Rover cars climbed about 6 percent thanks to strong demand for the Rover 400 and the MGF sports car.
As BMW had hoped, Rover was less dependent on the British market, with strong growth in foreign market such as Germany, Italy and North America.

Many analysts have feared that Rover, which BMW bought in 1994, would consume an ever-larger share of the company's profits, but the Munich-based carmaker said investment so far this year climbed 7 to 8 percent for both BMW and Rover -- a steady level already part of its long-term plans.
